### Add jvmcontract, a Rust library and CLI for the verifiers

[`9c742ae6cdab`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/9c742ae6cdab2574e7626e5d8b0eee169c141333) · [log `e3f0a086ef4e`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/e3f0a086ef4ed58298ff8b082bc197ef3ca34408ad53d16f942a211eb5e2027b.jsonl.gz)

New top-level lib/: the jvmcontract crate, a port of the Java contract verifier (behavioural, regression and capability contracts) and of the TLA+ generator and TLC runner in the examples tooling, with enhancements. Behavioural contracts are now derived without a JVM: the crate parses class files, reads the JDK's own classes from its lib/modules image, and executes every input of the finite domain in a built-in bytecode interpreter that models the JDK natively and refuses anything it does not model. The interpreter carries a dynamic effect monitor (every heap object remembers the epoch it was allocated in; a write to an older object makes the method unverifiable), which makes the purity proof complete over the executed domain and closes the array/collection-store gap the Java tool documented. Regression proofs generate the JBMC harness directly as bytecode, with the --unchanged-unless expression parsed, type-checked and compiled by the crate, so no Java compiler is in the pipeline; counterexamples are replayed in the interpreter. New contract kinds and views: instance methods of finite types (the receiver as a domain dimension), API contracts (the public surface of a module), per-dependency capability contracts, a Mermaid/Graphviz state-machine view of a contract, a TLC runner that parses verdicts and traces into data, JSON output, execution cost and step/depth budgets. The setup installer and doctor gain the Rust toolchain; the main README and approaches.md point at lib/.

Verified: cargo test (27 unit tests, 16 integration tests over javac-compiled fixtures) passes with zero clippy warnings. The integration tests derive the Box Office OrderLifecycle#decide contract and the ticketing-domain capability contract and check them identical to the files the Java tool committed, generate the TLA+ operator and check it identical to the one the Python generator wrote, run TLC on the Box Office model (verified, 4,732 states), and run the three JBMC scenarios of the Java tests (a rounding refactor refuted with a replayed counterexample, a scoped change proved, the same change refuted without the scope). The generated harness was also run on HotSpot with -Xverify:all. A release-build derivation of the 36-case contract takes about 15 ms.

### Add Quorum, ten distributed-systems examples, and property proofs to jvmcontract

[`3ce18250a348`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/3ce18250a348ef68dde6c1fd3786a8abe6525576) · [log `60d86acb58f4`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/60d86acb58f45e9afa8db5ba7027d3b3b47a4258e4be27f9ae025c1a088012bc.jsonl.gz)

A second subject system, examples/apps/quorum: the pure decision kernels of a replicated system (Raft's vote rule and role machine, majority quorums, exponential backoff, a hybrid logical clock, last-writer-wins resolution and a two-phase-commit coordinator with a TLA+ model of the protocol around it). It is plain javac with a reflective test runner, no Gradle, and it is verified by the Rust tool: behavioural, capability and API contracts, a properties file, and TLC on the model; verify.sh runs all of it in seconds.

jvmcontract gains 'prove', a property proof by bounded model checking: a Java boolean expression over a method's parameters, its result and calls of the method itself (so laws such as commutativity or antisymmetry can be stated), optionally restricted by an assumption, generated as a bytecode harness and proved by JBMC over every input or refuted with an input replayed in the interpreter. 'prove --properties FILE' proves every block of a committed properties.contract as a build step. The expression language gained calls and a comma token; the verifier skips the properties file; a new SARIF rule property-violated. A bug found on the way: JBMC runs in the work directory, so a relative class path entry silently became a stub with an arbitrary result and every property was refuted with nonsense witnesses; class path entries are now made absolute and JBMC's 'failed to access directory' warning is an unverifiable verdict, with unit tests for both.

Examples 013 to 022 run the Rust tool over Quorum: a longest-log-wins vote rule refuted by regression proof over 2^448 inputs (013); a leader that ignores newer terms in replies, one changed case of 52 with the state machine drawn (014); (n+1)/2 refuted as a majority at n=2 (015); a backoff cleanup whose shift overflows into a negative delay (016); a hybrid logical clock refactor proved monotonic and symmetric (017) and one that drops a case, refuted (018); jitter that gives the module a randomness capability (019); a 2PC coordinator that presumes commit on timeout, a three-step TLC trace where the one vote cast is a no still in flight (020); abort-on-first-no proved safe in 644 states (021); and a skew-tolerant last-writer-wins tie-break that breaks antisymmetry (022). build.py got a runner table per subject app, the B11 approach, a Mermaid state-machine view for state-machine contracts, and TLC through 'jvmcontract tlc --json'. Verified by running the generator (all ten verdicts as expected, about 20 s in all), cargo test (30 unit, 18 integration tests), clippy clean, and verify.sh.

### Add Crosscut, eleven Spring Boot examples verified by jvmcontract

[`c9ff761a7aea`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/c9ff761a7aeaaa082efefe67192bdf8bcf77f462) · [log `a1f98f08719c`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/a1f98f08719cef459d009ebf2b94c6fc91023fbcaea37a277e60ea9f5fee185f.jsonl.gz)

A third subject system, examples/apps/crosscut: the pure kernels behind a Spring Boot service's cross-cutting concerns, written so that jvmcontract can prove them. TransactionBoundary (the propagation and rollback rules of a transaction interceptor, two behavioural contracts of 16 and 22 cases), CircuitBreaker (44 cases, drawn as a state machine), RetryPolicy, TokenBucket, IdempotentReceiver (24 cases, plus a TLA+ model of a client retrying against it, 168 states), a Kafka Partitioner and BatchCommit, JwtTimestamps and cache Expiry. The module has capability and API contracts, seven properties proved by JBMC in about forty seconds, plain javac tests and a verify.sh.

Examples 023 to 033 run eleven changes to it through the tool: Math.abs in a partitioner (023, B11), clock skew on the wrong side of nbf (024, B11), a rollback rule that commits after an Error (025, B8), a half-open breaker that closes on the first good probe (026, B8), a switch rewrite of the retry policy that drops the unlisted 5xx (027, B9), a Thread.sleep added to the retry policy (028, B10), an idempotency key that executes a retry while the first attempt is in flight (029, D1, five-step trace), stored failures proved at-most-once (030, D1, verified), a token bucket that stamps refills with now (031, B11, caught by one test), a batch listener that commits past a failed record (032, B11) and a cache expiry rewritten as a deadline proved on every nanosecond (033, B11, verified). Nine of the eleven are missed by the module's tests.

build.py now has a table of javac apps (TOOL_APPS, TOOL_MODELS) instead of Quorum-specific functions, and reads a contract's case count from the output line that names the symbol, since a module with several contracts prints one line each. A money-allocation kernel was tried and dropped: JBMC's SAT backend cannot prove identities between divisions and multiplications (the sum of floorDiv shares) in minutes; approaches.md and the lib README record the limit. Verified by running the eleven examples (all verdicts as expected, about 20 seconds), examples/apps/crosscut/verify.sh (39 tests, 4 contracts, 7 properties, TLC), and three Quorum examples through the refactored generator.

### Add Mica, twelve JVM-kernel examples, and four jvmcontract fixes

[`172a4d4331e3`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/172a4d4331e34875d89054b0a25c25da51ac7022) · [log `dc606bccc33d`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/dc606bccc33d40e4bca77ace0bb4f9b3bf165f3d771f1fcf9e03544a58fc061c.jsonl.gz)

Mica (examples/apps/mica) is a fourth subject system: the decision kernels of a small JVM written in Java, each the few lines where the JVM specification says exactly what must happen. Class initialization (JVMS 5.5) as a state machine with a TLA+ model of threads racing for one class, checked by TLC with deadlock detection; the type checker's isAssignable over sixteen verification types (289-case contract); access control at resolution (5.4.4, 120 cases, with and without nestmates); idiv and irem at Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1; fcmpg/fcmpl with NaN; the bisection of a lookupswitch; javac's tableswitch/lookupswitch cost heuristic; a power-of-two table size; and the modified UTF-8 of the constant pool. Six properties prove in under two seconds; the whole verify.sh runs in about three.

Examples 034 to 045 are one realistic change each, for readers who work on the JVM or the libraries closest to it: an idiv that throws where the specification returns the dividend (034), a NaN check written as == Float.NaN (035), javac's switch costs computed in int (036), the JDK 11 tableSizeFor rewrite proved equal on all 2^32 inputs (037), a verifier fast path that lets an uninitialized object pass as an Object (038), protected access without the receiver rule (039), JEP 181 nestmate access as a four-line contract diff (040), StrictMath intrinsics looked up through MethodHandles (041), a class initialization that lets other threads proceed during &lt;clinit> (042) and one that waits on its own thread, which TLC reports as a deadlock (043), modified UTF-8 with a one-byte NUL (044), and (low + high) / 2 proved safe within a Code attribute's bounds (045). Nine violations, three verified; every violation is missed by the module's tests.

The tool needed four changes, found while writing the examples: JBMC's witness syntax for chars ('\u0000') and floats (Float.NaN, the infinities) is parsed, and chars are shown as Java literals; java.lang.Integer, Long, Short and Byte join Math and StrictMath on JBMC's class path, taken from the JDK image, so Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros is analysed as written; a counterexample that the interpreter cannot reproduce (both versions agree, or the property holds on replay) is reported as unverifiable instead of a false violation, which is what a stubbed JDK method such as Float.compare produced before; and jvmcontract tlc gains --deadlock, with TLC's deadlock trace parsed and reported like an invariant violation. build.py gets the app and its model (with the deadlock flag and prose), and the docs the fourth system.

Verified by: the Mica tests (47) and verify.sh; build.py for 034 to 045 (every verdict as expected) and for 013 to 033 rerun under the changed tool (unchanged apart from timestamps and TLC seeds, restored); cargo test (50 tests, JBMC and TLC included).

llm-dlc/tools/feature-loop.sh resumes session 360e8b8b on Fable 5.1 at high effort and repeats one instruction from the repo root: add more advanced features and examples to jvmcontract. Each cycle that produces a commit is followed by /compact and another cycle. A cycle with no new commit stops the loop with exit 1, before compacting, so the session keeps its full context for whoever looks into it. ### Add array properties with JML quantifiers, and three Mica examples

[`ea9bd8c93383`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/ea9bd8c933838725bd3751995fd1b6543af358c3) · [log `84b6ab145c65`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/84b6ab145c657124fdeb46d451eb2164188f77324398cc25e32ca2ebfe026b09.jsonl.gz)

jvmcontract prove now takes array parameters and array results of integral or boolean element type. The property language gained a.length, a[index], and JML's bounded quantifiers (\forall int i; range; body) and (\exists ...), where the range must bound the variable below and above and any other conjunct filters. A quantifier is compiled to a loop in the generated bytecode harness (CodeBuilder gained iinc) and evaluated as a loop for the replay guard. Array arguments are symbolic arrays of every length up to --max-array-length (8 by default, or arrays: N per block in properties.contract), never null; JBMC's array inputs are parsed from the trace (the object's length and data fields and the data array's elements before the INPUT line, elements with their (byte) casts), replayed through the interpreter, rendered as [1, 2, 3], and an array parameter is read after the call, as the harness reads it, so a method that writes into a buffer is held to what it wrote (the witness shows the array it left). An exception thrown while evaluating the assertion, such as an index out of bounds, fails the property and the replay says so. The replay guard no longer runs on assertions that call the method under proof, which only the harness can evaluate.

Mica gained ExceptionTable.handlerIndex (JVMS 4.7.3 and 2.10) and ModifiedUtf8.encodeInto, with tests, API and capability contracts regenerated, and three properties: the lookupswitch bisection finds every key in every sorted table and returns -1 exactly when the key is absent; the exception-table entry found covers the pc in [start_pc, end_pc); no byte the encoder writes is zero or in 0xf0 to 0xff. Examples 046 (the search rewritten half-open, proved), 047 (an inclusive end_pc, refuted at the boundary) and 048 (supplementary characters in four bytes, refuted on a surrogate pair) run through build.py; 044's patch was rebased onto the changed encoder file. The READMEs describe the quantifiers and the measured limits of JBMC's SAT backend on arrays: a quantifier that repeats a linear scan's comparisons (that the entry found is the first, or that -1 means no match) did not finish in minutes even on four entries or with z3, eight symbolic writes followed by a quantifier take minutes where three take a second, and a method allocating new byte[n] with n computed from the data never finished.

### Add generalized JML quantifiers, witness shrinking, and four Mica examples

[`9d27af14b14f`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/9d27af14b14f251149398140d3ef2bcc3d113230) · [log `e2060f74aa0e`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/e2060f74aa0e5c5f33cd23f62dde6188b8ac3ee9e0aca7244b319efab8d75f9c.jsonl.gz)

The property language of jvmcontract prove gains JML's generalized quantifiers \sum, \num_of, \max and \min, which fold a value over a bounded range (an int or long sum wrapping as Java does, a count, an extreme with JML's values over an empty range), compiled to accumulator loops in the generated bytecode harness and evaluated in the interpreter; they nest, so max_stack is stated as a \max over a \sum. An array parameter can now be passed by name to a call of the method under proof, which is how a law about the previous element is stated (offsetOf(offsetDelta, k - 1)).

A refuting input found by JBMC is shrunk before it is reported: the generated PropertyHarness class is run in the interpreter on smaller inputs, dropping array elements (one array at a time, then the same index from every array), and moving numbers towards zero by powers of two, while the property still fails, up to 4000 runs. The witness on the page is that local minimum, the same on every run; the report keeps JBMC's input and the run count, and --no-shrink turns it off. Example 047's witness went from an eight-entry table of nine-digit numbers to one entry [0, 0) at pc 0, and 048's to the first surrogate pair.

Mica gains four kernels with tests and properties: StackMapTable.offsetOf (frame k is at k plus the sum of the deltas, and above the previous frame), CodeAttribute.attributeLength (a \sum over the nested attributes with their six-byte headers), ConstantPool.indexOf (1 + entry + the \num_of long and double entries before it) and asm.MaxStack.of (the largest prefix sum). Examples 049 to 052: a stack map loop without the first-frame special case, proved; a Code attribute length that drops the nested headers, refuted and shrunk to one empty attribute; a constant pool numbering that counts the long entry itself, refuted on a one-entry pool; and a max_stack that checks the depth only after a push, proved under the assumption that stack effects lie in -255 to 2, which the proof itself demanded: over every int effect the argument fails on a wrapping sum. Measured and recorded in the README: a sum is exponential for the SAT backend when the kernel accumulates in a different association than the property (bound 4 took 80 s, 6 never finished) and nine seconds at bound 8 when the orders match.

Verified by cargo test (40 unit, 20 integration, including new fixtures for sums, counts and maxima and a test that refuted witnesses come back shrunk), by examples/apps/mica/verify.sh (65 tests, three contracts, thirteen properties, TLC), and by regenerating every B11 example page, 013 to 052, with the expected verdicts.

### Add throws clauses to property proofs, and two Mica examples

[`e3b6332db581`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/e3b6332db5813dc2909b09c771b0b6aee03151ec) · [log `40223b5f7138`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/40223b5f7138a5cc18636775655e2613c0f3499e3e7367d94a009ecc9ab4cba2.jsonl.gz)

A property may now declare the exceptional behaviour of the method it is about, as JML's signals clause does: `throws: ArithmeticException when divisor == 0` in properties.contract, or `--throws` on the command line, repeatable. The generated harness computes before the call which clause applies (the first whose condition holds), catches the declared class before the generic ones, and asserts that the method threw that exception exactly where a clause applies and returned with the assertion holding everywhere else. A void method's property can be its throws clauses alone. A declared JDK exception JBMC has no model of (ClassFormatError) is taken from the JDK image with its superclasses up to one JBMC models. A refutation says what the clause required of the input, the declared exception or a normal return, and the replay guard accepts a thrown instance of the expected class as the property holding.

Witness shrinking gained a step for values a property ties together: every positive integral value, scalar or array element, moves down by the same amount (and every negative one up), so an end equal to a length or a pc equal to an entry's end reaches zero together instead of stopping at the solver's numbers.

Mica: idiv and irem now declare ArithmeticException on a zero divisor instead of assuming it away, and a new ExceptionTable.checkEntry kernel checks an exception table entry as JVMS 4.7.3 requires, with a ClassFormatError clause as its whole property. Example 053 removes the explicit zero check from idiv and irem and is proved to throw exactly where the host does; example 054 compares end_pc like the other offsets and is refuted on a one-byte method whose handler covers it, a change the tests miss. Example 034's explanation was reworded for the clause, build.py parses the clauses and the expected outcome into the pages, the result schema allows them, and the B11 pages were regenerated.

Verified with cargo test (42 unit, 21 integration, including a new test that proves and refutes clauses on IllegalArgumentException and on ClassFormatError), clippy clean, examples/apps/mica/verify.sh (68 tests, 14 properties, TLC), and examples/tools/build.py on every B11 example with the expected verdicts.

### Add JML \old to property proofs, and two Mica examples

[`fecdf6eda270`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/fecdf6eda270c092b27d95ef6b2829531bdc25b0) · [log `9282ed25a83a`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/9282ed25a83ab4efe045a2ab1e83991102abb2bc96554fecad2dc8f0f2f9b47c.jsonl.gz)

Property proofs can now state what a method did to an array parameter against what it received, with JML's pre-state operator: \old(a[i]) is the element before the call, from a copy the generated harness takes first, so a frame condition such as (\forall int i; result &lt;= i && i &lt; out.length; out[i] == \old(out[i])) and a permutation property for an in-place sort are expressible. \old(a.length) reads the array itself (lengths do not change), \old(x) of a scalar is x, and \old of result or inside an assumption or throws condition is an error. The copy is allocated at the bound on the arrays rather than the array's symbolic length, which the solver handles about thirty times faster (a six-element reversal: 98 s with an exact copy, 2.8 s with the bounded one); only a copy passed to a call of the method under proof is exact. The replay guard evaluates \old over the input as JBMC gave it.

A block of properties.contract may now set unwind: N, the loop unwinding bound for that property, because a quadratic method under a quadratic quantifier (an insertion sort of four pairs proved a pair-preserving permutation) finishes in fifteen seconds unwound five times and not in minutes at the default sixteen.

Mica gained SwitchLowering.sortPairs, the sort of a lookupswitch's match-offset pairs (JVMS 6.5), with a throws clause, arrays: 4 and unwind: 5, and the encoder's property gained the frame conjunct; the API and capability contracts were regenerated for the new method. Example 055 is an encoder that zero-terminates the string into the caller's buffer, refuted on encodeInto(chars=[], out=[-1]); example 056 is a sort whose comparison is the difference of the keys, refuted on two keys just over 2^31 apart that it swaps. Both pass the existing tests. Example 048's page was regenerated with the extended property; the other B11 pages were regenerated and differ only in timings, so they were restored.

Verified with cargo test (44 unit tests, 22 integration tests, one new over a fixture with an in-place reversal, a buggy zeroing and a pair sort), clippy clean, Mica's verify.sh (71 tests, three contracts, sixteen properties in about a minute and a half, TLC 37 states, no deadlock) and build.py over every B11 example, each with its expected verdict.

### Cap the feature loop's memory with a systemd scope

[`6a5a1237de76`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/6a5a1237de760dc5152339e5eaed718902794ad4) · [log `f61f985aeeaf`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/f61f985aeeaf00da9b1d4b651a65159ae61895592d12608bf585774669b9ae7c.jsonl.gz)

The feature loop ran as part of init.scope, the cgroup WSL shells start in, so a memory-hungry proof could exhaust the machine and take the WSL instance down. feature-loop.sh now re-executes itself in feature-loop.scope with a 4 GB cap (FEATURE_LOOP_MEMORY_MAX) and no swap. It sets OOMPolicy=continue because the default stops the entire scope on the first kill, which would take claude down with the proof. It refuses to start when less memory than the cap is available or when the scope is still active.

Verified by running the real script with a stub claude on PATH under a 100M cap: the memory hog was killed with status 137, the stub survived, and the loop exited 1 through its usual no-commit path. Also checked refusal for a cap above available memory, an invalid cap and a second concurrent loop, exit 130 on systemctl stop, and that the scope unloads afterwards. A real proof run under the cap was not tested. The separate lib/ work in progress is left out of this commit.

### Add regression proofs over arrays

[`9c482d83ea46`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/9c482d83ea46ffa736d8583dd7def725659ca83b) · [log `f61f985aeeaf`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/f61f985aeeaf00da9b1d4b651a65159ae61895592d12608bf585774669b9ae7c.jsonl.gz)

jvmcontract equivalence now accepts methods with array parameters and results. The harness copies each array argument exactly as long, runs the previous version on the copies and the new one on the originals, and compares results, exceptions and what each version leaves in the arrays, element by element, with two NaN results counting as equal. The scope in --unchanged-unless may quantify over an array. A differing input is shrunk in the interpreter and reported with what each version left behind. Replay and shrinking moved out of property.rs into a shared witness module. New options are --max-array-length and --no-shrink.

Verified with javac and jbmc on the PATH: all 71 tests pass, including the regression test over arrays, and clippy is clean. Written by the unattended feature loop before the crash; committed separately after the memory limits.

## What I built

A new top-level `lib/` holds `jvmcontract`, a Rust crate and command line (the name is free on crates.io). It ports everything the Java verifier and the Python scripts did, and the committed Box Office artifacts prove the port: the derived `OrderLifecycle.decide.contract`, the `capabilities.contract`, and the generated `OrderLifecycleContract.tla` are identical to the files already in the repo, which the test suite checks.

**Ported.** Behavioural contracts (B8), regression proofs with JBMC (B9), capability contracts (B10), the TLA+ operator generator and a TLC runner (D1), SARIF output, and the `verify`/`update` workflow with the same file formats and options, so the Gradle plugin can run either tool.

**Beyond the port.**
- **No JVM.** Contracts are derived by a built-in bytecode interpreter with native models of the JDK; the JDK's own class shapes are read straight from `lib/modules` (only its index is loaded). A full derivation takes about 15 ms in a release build, versus a Gradle build plus JVM start before.

## Two features

**Generalized quantifiers.** The property language now has JML's `\sum`, `\num_of`, `\max` and `\min` next to `\forall` and `\exists`. Each folds a value over a bounded range and becomes an accumulator loop in the generated bytecode harness. They nest, so an assembler's `max_stack` is stated as its definition:
